evidence_set: 21 cohorts (12 alcohol, 4 heroin, 5 polysubstance) published 2000–2015: follow-up 3 to 50 years (mean 17, median 13); remission required for 6 months to 10 years; 7 cohorts required abstinence and 14 accepted controlled use; 15 clinical, 4 community and 2 general-population samples.
Methods › 2.1, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2); Results › 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (PDF pp. 3–4); Discussion, 7th paragraph (starting PDF p. 10; sample types on p. 11)

Standard rate 0.511 in the 15 cohorts with all or most people in treatment at baseline against 0.624 in the 6 without (two of them population samples in which some people were in treatment), p 0.421; no significant difference by substance either (alcohol 0.517, heroin 0.540, polysubstance 0.609); only treatment at baseline was analysed, and the Discussion lists treatment received over time among characteristics not tested.
Results › 3.3, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 7); Table 2 and footnotes (PDF p. 8); Discussion, 7th paragraph (starting PDF p. 10; treatment over time on p. 11)

The authors conclude that remitted-sample estimates (method 3), the commonest kind, do not suit treatment planning because they start from people already in remission and so not in need of treatment, and note that a majority of studies defined remission over 6–12 months, so the review's estimates suit planning over one year.
